449.title: Shelach: forty years (Numbers 14:33–34)
449.hook: a year for each day of scouting; a new generation will enter
449.howItsDone: The forty years in the wilderness are read in Shelach each summer; the Talmud links the night of weeping after the scouts' report to the ninth of Av, the fast day that mourns the destruction of the Temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday Caleb had another spirit, and your line was a different spirit. Did your we can sentence get said out loud? Today, what the night of weeping costs. Day four hundred forty-nine.

Forty days of scouting. That's how long the trip into the land took: about the length of a long summer break. Forty days of walking hills, cutting grapes, sizing up walls. Then one bad night of fear. And the answer that comes back from God is a number that sounds almost impossible. Not forty days of delay. Forty years. Long enough for a toddler to become a grandparent. Long enough that most of the people standing in that camp, listening, will never see the land at all. Today: the longest detour in the Torah, and why.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OF SCOUTING.` → `ONE NIGHT OF FEAR.` → `FORTY YEARS.`

segments.voice: Numbers fourteen. The people have cried all night that they'd rather have died in Egypt, or in the wilderness. God answers them, in a sense, with their own words. In this wilderness, the generation that was counted, from twenty years old and up, will live out their lives. Forty days you scouted the land, the verse says, "for every day a year". Forty years in the wilderness. Except Caleb and Joshua. And then a line with a sting and a promise in it: your little ones, the children you said would be taken as prey, them I will bring in. The children the parents were afraid for become the generation that enters. Is it a punishment, or something more? Both readings are in the tradition. The text calls it bearing their iniquity. But medieval commentators like Ibn Ezra and Maimonides add another layer. People raised as slaves, they suggest, learned to bow their heads. It takes a generation raised in freedom, in the open wilderness, eating manna, to have the courage to go up. Change on that scale doesn't happen in forty days. And the very next morning, the people try anyway: we'll go up now, they say. Moses warns them that God isn't with them in it. They go, and they're beaten back. You can't shortcut the forty years by a burst of nerve. The Talmud adds that this night of weeping fell on the ninth of Av, which later became the saddest day of the Jewish calendar.
screen: `FOR EVERY DAY A YEAR.` · `YOUR LITTLE ONES WILL ENTER.` · `A GENERATION RAISED FREE.` · `THE NEXT MORNING'S SHORTCUT FAILS.` · then, large: `CHANGE TAKES A GENERATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one slow road. Breathe, and think of a change you want that keeps not arriving: a habit, a family pattern, a community, yourself. Notice the part of you that wants it in forty days. Then picture it taking years, and you still walking toward it. Not giving up; walking. Ask what small daily thing belongs to the long road, the way manna fell every morning. Let it be slow. The bell holds the time.
Shelach, the scouts' portion: forty days of looking, one night of fear, and forty years for a free generation to grow up.
Your line: change takes a generation. Today, do one small thing for a slow change you won't finish this year, and do it anyway. Day four hundred forty-nine.

450.title: Shelach: the fringes (Numbers 15:37–41)
450.hook: fringes on the corners of garments, to look upon and remember
450.howItsDone: Some Jews wear tzitzit daily on a four-cornered undergarment and on the tallit, the prayer shawl; at morning prayer, during the Shema, people gather the fringes and kiss them when the word tzitzit is said.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forty years, and your line, change takes a generation. Did a slow change get one small step? Today, the last paragraph of the scouts' portion. Day four hundred fifty.

A string tied around a finger. A sticky note on the bathroom mirror. A hair tie on the wrong wrist so you don't forget to call your mom back. Little physical things hold on to big intentions, the kind that slide off the mind by lunchtime. The Torah has one too, and it hangs off the corners of clothes, in synagogues and on ordinary sidewalks. Watch someone at morning prayer gather a handful of white strings and press them to their lips. That's today's word.
screen: `A STRING AROUND A FINGER.` → `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `STRINGS ON THE CORNERS.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses: speak to the children of Israel, and have them make fringes on the corners of their garments, through all their generations, with a thread of blue on each corner fringe. The fringe is called tzitzit. And here's what it's for: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them". Look, remember, do. A chain from the eye to the hands. Then the verse adds: and don't go wandering after your own heart and your own eyes. The Hebrew verb there is lo taturu, don't scout around. It's the same verb used for the scouts. Some readers hear that echo as the reason this paragraph closes the scouts' portion. Rashi says the heart and the eyes are the body's scouts: the eye sees, the heart wants, the body follows. The scouts let their eyes and fears lead them. The fringes are a counter-scout, hanging right at your side. Rashi also counts the word itself. The letters of tzitzit add up to six hundred; add the eight strings and five knots on each corner, and you get six hundred thirteen, the traditional number of the commandments. Tradition says the blue came from a dye made from a sea creature, and that the knowledge of making it was lost, so most tzitzit are all white; some people today use a blue they believe has been recovered. Some Jews wear tzitzit every day, under or over their shirts, and on a prayer shawl. And in traditional prayer this paragraph is said morning and evening, as the last part of the Shema.
screen: `FRINGES ON THE CORNERS.` · `LOOK, REMEMBER, DO.` · `LO TATURU: DON'T SCOUT AROUND.` · `600 + 8 + 5 = 613.` · then, large: `SEE AND REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie a knot to remember something. Find something you can tie: a thread, a shoelace, a strip of paper, the drawstring on your hoodie. Choose one thing you want to remember today, a person to call, a promise, a way you want to treat people. Say it to yourself. Then tie the knot slowly, while you hold the thought. Look at it. Let the knot hold the memory, so your mind doesn't have to grip it alone. The bell holds the time.
Tzitzit. The fringes: strings on the corners of a garment, to look at, remember, and do.
Your line: see and remember. Each time you see your knot today, remember what you tied into it, and do one thing about it. Day four hundred fifty.

451.title: Korach: sounds fair (Numbers 16:3)
451.hook: Korach says all the congregation is holy; the words are true, the motive is not
451.howItsDone: When the portion Korach is read, Jewish teachers often pair Korach's speech with the midrash of the all-blue cloak, and use it to talk about the difference between a true claim and the reason someone is making it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzitzit, the fringes, and your line, see and remember. Did your knot remind you of something, and did you act on it? Hold on to those fringes. They come back today, in an argument. Day four hundred fifty-one.

A speech can be built entirely out of true sentences. Everyone deserves a voice. The people in charge have been there too long. Why should a few decide for everyone? A listener can agree with every word and still sense something off, once they notice who's speaking, and what that person would get if they won. This week's portion opens with exactly that kind of speech. It's delivered to Moses' face, in front of a crowd, by his own cousin. And the line at the center of it is hard to argue with.
screen: `A SPEECH MADE OF TRUE SENTENCES.` → `WHO'S SPEAKING?` → `MOSES' OWN COUSIN.`

segments.voice: Korach is a Levite, a grandson of Kohath, from the same family as Moses and Aaron. He gathers Dathan and Abiram, and two hundred fifty respected leaders, and they confront Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them; wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?" Every phrase has a source. At Sinai, God called the whole people a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. In Leviticus, holiness was spoken to the whole congregation. Korach's words echo the Torah back at Moses. So what's wrong? The rabbis looked under the speech. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says Korach was jealous: a younger cousin had been appointed leader of their clan instead of him. And a midrash pictures his opening move. He dresses his followers in cloaks made entirely of blue wool, and asks Moses: does a cloak that's all blue still need a blue thread in its fringes? Moses says yes. Korach's crowd laughs. A whole garment of blue, and you still need one thread? He's using yesterday's commandment to make both the law and Moses look ridiculous. Then Moses answers, and he exposes the motive. You Levites, he says, isn't it enough that you serve at the sanctuary? Now you want the priesthood too? Moses even hands Korach's words back to him: you take too much upon you. In the rabbis' reading, the claim was that everyone is equal. The goal was to be above.
screen: `ALL THE CONGREGATION ARE HOLY.` · `TRUE WORDS, FROM THE TORAH.` · `A CLOAK ALL OF BLUE.` · `NOW YOU WANT THE PRIESTHOOD TOO?` · then, large: `WHAT'S UNDER THE ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check your motive in one argument. Breathe, and bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now: at work, at home, online. Say your position to yourself in its best words. Then ask, quietly: what do I get if I win? Respect? Being right? A seat I've wanted? Revenge for an old slight? Don't judge what you find. Just look under the argument, the way the rabbis looked under Korach's. Notice whether the words and the want point the same way. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The Levite who said all the congregation is holy, true words, carried by a wish to be above them.
Your line: what's under the argument. Today, before you make your next point in a disagreement, name to yourself what you want from winning. Day four hundred fifty-one.

452.title: Korach: not for heaven's sake (Avot 5:17)
452.hook: the Mishnah names Korach's quarrel as the dispute not for heaven's sake
452.tomorrow: Korach: Moses falls on his face
452.howItsDone: By custom, Pirkei Avot is studied a chapter at a time on Shabbat afternoons in the weeks after Passover, and in some communities through the summer, so this teaching about arguments comes around again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Korach said the whole congregation is holy, which is true, and used it to reach for power. Your line was what's under the argument. Did you catch a motive hiding under a good point? Day four hundred fifty-two.

Some arguments are over by Friday, and nobody remembers what they were about. Others are still being studied, word by word, long after everyone in them has died. The Mishnah, in the collection called Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, sorts disputes into two piles. It gives each pile one example. For the good pile, two teachers whose schools disagreed again and again. For the other pile, the rebel we met yesterday. Korach. Today: what makes an argument worth keeping.
screen: `SOME ARGUMENTS END BY FRIDAY.` → `SOME ARE STILL STUDIED.` → `TWO PILES, TWO EXAMPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the teaching, in paraphrase. Every dispute that is for the sake of heaven will in the end endure. Every dispute that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure. Which dispute was for the sake of heaven? The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. Which was not? The dispute of Korach and all his company. The Hebrew phrase is l'shem shamayim, for the name of heaven. It means an argument whose goal is the truth, not the person arguing. Hillel and Shammai each left a school of students, and the two schools argued over question after question of Jewish law. The Talmud says a heavenly voice finally declared that both schools speak the words of the living God, and that the law follows Hillel's school. The reason it gives is not that they were cleverer. They were patient and humble, they taught the other school's view along with their own, and they even mentioned Shammai's view first. Those arguments are still printed and studied today. That's what endure means. Now look at the other half of the line. It doesn't say the dispute of Korach and Moses. It says Korach and his company. Commentators noticed this. In their reading, Moses wasn't fighting for himself at all. And some add that Korach's allies each wanted something different, so a fight that's about winning ends up turning on itself. Some teachers draw a simple test from this: in an argument for heaven's sake, you'd be glad if the other side turned out right, because then the truth won.
screen: `TWO PILES OF ARGUMENTS.` · `L'SHEM SHAMAYIM: FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.` · `HILLEL AND SHAMMAI: STILL STUDIED.` · `KORACH AND HIS COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: argue for truth, not for winning. Settle, and breathe. This time, start with the other side. Bring to mind someone you disagree with, about anything, large or small. Find the strongest thing they've said, and put it into words as fairly as they would, maybe better. Then ask one quiet question: if they turned out to be right, could I live with that? You don't have to change your mind. Just notice which pile this argument belongs in today. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The rebel the Mishnah chose as its example of a dispute not for heaven's sake, set beside Hillel and Shammai, whose arguments endure.
Your line: not for heaven's sake. Today, in one conversation, say the other person's best point back to them before you make yours. Day four hundred fifty-two.

453.title: Korach: Moses falls on his face (Numbers 16:4)
453.hook: attacked, Moses first falls on his face before answering
453.tomorrow: Korach: the man who went home
453.howItsDone: In traditional weekday prayer, a short section called tachanun is said with the head resting on the arm, and its traditional name, nefilat apayim, falling on the face, echoes the way Moses and Aaron fell on their faces in the wilderness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah set Korach's quarrel beside Hillel and Shammai's, as the argument that doesn't last. Your line was not for heaven's sake. Did you catch yourself wanting the win more than the truth? Day four hundred fifty-three.

The message arrives at 11pm. It's sharp, it's public, and half of it is unfair. Thumbs start moving before the mind catches up. A reply sent in that moment can look very different by morning. In the Torah, Korach and two hundred and fifty leaders of the community gather against Moses and Aaron and accuse them, to their faces, of lifting themselves above everyone else. It's an attack on Moses' whole life's work. Everyone waits for his answer. Before he says a single word, he does something else.
screen: `A SHARP MESSAGE AT 11PM.` → `KORACH GATHERS AGAINST MOSES.` → `EVERYONE WAITS FOR HIS ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The verse is very short. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face." In Hebrew, that's va-yipol al panav. He drops to the ground, face down, in front of the crowd. The Torah doesn't explain why. The commentators fill the silence in different ways. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, reads it as distress: this was not the first time the people had turned on him, and Moses felt he had little left to say on their behalf. Others read it as prayer, a way of turning to God before turning to the people. Either way, notice the order. First he falls silent. Then he speaks. And when he does speak, he doesn't answer the insult. He says, in paraphrase, in the morning the Lord will show who is His. In the morning. He gives the night a chance. Rashi suggests Moses hoped that with a few hours, they might think again. Then Moses sends for two of the leading rebels, Dathan and Abiram, to talk. They refuse to come. But he tried. It's worth knowing that Moses falls on his face again and again in the book of Numbers: when the people despair after the scouts' report, and twice more during this very rebellion, pleading for the people's lives. It becomes a pattern when things fall apart. Not a weapon. A pause, with his face to the ground, before anything else.
screen: `HE FELL UPON HIS FACE.` · `DISTRESS, OR PRAYER, OR BOTH.` · `IN THE MORNING: TIME TO THINK AGAIN.` · `HIS FIRST MOVE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause before replying to an attack. Settle, and lower your eyes, or close them. Bring to mind a time someone came at you with words: last week, or years ago. Notice how fast the answer wanted to come. Now, instead of answering, just let your head bow a little. Breathe in. Breathe out. Let the reply wait. See whether the silence gives you some room. If a better answer comes, keep it for later. Stay with your breath until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The rebellion that brought Moses to the ground before it brought him to his feet, falling on his face first, then answering.
Your line: fall silent first. Today, when a message stings, put the phone face down for one full breath before you write back. Day four hundred fifty-three.

454.title: Korach: the man who went home (Sanhedrin 109b)
454.hook: On ben Peleth vanishes from the rebellion; the Talmud says his wife talked him out of it
454.howItsDone: The story of On ben Peleth and his wife is a well-known Talmudic teaching that is often told when the portion of Korach is read in synagogue in early summer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, attacked in front of everyone, Moses fell on his face before he said a word. Your line was fall silent first. Did you manage one breath before a reply? Day four hundred fifty-four.

Read the first verse of the Korach story slowly and you'll find a roll call. Korach. Dathan and Abiram. And one more: On, the son of Peleth. He's right there at the start of the rebellion, named with the leaders. Then he's gone. When the trouble comes to its terrible end, Korach, Dathan and Abiram are all named again. On never appears again, anywhere in the Bible. Readers noticed the gap a long time ago. What happened to the fourth man? The Talmud has an answer, and it's a story about a kitchen-table conversation.
screen: `A ROLL CALL OF REBELS.` → `ON, THE SON OF PELETH.` → `THEN HE'S GONE.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, and here it is in paraphrase. On's wife asks him a simple question. What do you get out of this? If Moses stays the leader, you're a follower. If Korach becomes the leader, you're still a follower. On admits she's right, but says he's stuck: he was in the meeting, he gave his word, they're counting on him. So she says, in effect, leave it to me. She gives him wine, he falls asleep inside the tent, and she sits at the entrance, in a way that makes the men coming to fetch him turn back. By the time he wakes, the rebellion is over, and he's alive. The Talmud reads a verse from Proverbs over the scene: every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands. The wise woman is On's wife. And the foolish one? The same passage says Korach's wife egged him on, feeding his resentment of Moses. So two homes, two conversations, two endings. A few things are worth noticing. The Torah itself says nothing about any of this; the Talmud is answering a silence in the text. Her argument isn't about who's right. It's about him: this fight isn't yours, and it won't give you what you think. And On's problem, but I already gave my word, is one plenty of people know. Sometimes the bravest thing is letting someone who loves you talk you down from a fight you joined too fast.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU GET OUT OF THIS?` · `SHE SITS AT THE TENT'S ENTRANCE.` · `A WISE WOMAN BUILDS HER HOUSE.` · `THE TORAH IS SILENT; THE TALMUD ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone talk you down. Settle, and breathe. Think of the person in your life who's good at asking, what do you actually get out of this? A partner, a friend, a sibling, an old teacher. Picture their face. Now think of one fight you're in, or one you're tempted to join. Imagine telling them about it. What would they ask? Let the question sit with you, without defending yourself. If you're grateful for that person, let yourself feel it. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The rebellion that started with four named men, and ended, the Talmud says, with one of them asleep safely at home.
Your line: she saved him. Today, before you dig in on something, ask one person you trust what they think, and really listen. Day four hundred fifty-four.

455.title: Korach: the staff that blossomed (Numbers 17:16–24)
455.hook: Aaron's staff sprouts blossoms and ripe almonds overnight
455.howItsDone: The blossoming of Aaron's staff is read in synagogue as part of the portion of Korach, and later Jewish tradition counts the staff among the things kept beside the Ark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, On son of Peleth went home, because his wife asked him what this fight would ever give him. Your line was she saved him. Did someone you trust get a say today? Day four hundred fifty-five.

An almond tree in winter looks dead. Gray bark, bare branches, nothing. Then one week, while the cold is still hanging on, it's covered in white and pink blossom. Hold that picture against the end of the Korach story. The ground has opened, fire has come down, and a plague has swept the camp. The people are terrified, and they're still muttering about who gets to serve. God's final answer to the whole rebellion is not another disaster. It's a stick of dry wood, and what happens to it overnight.
screen: `AN ALMOND TREE IN WINTER.` → `AFTER THE GROUND, THE FIRE, THE PLAGUE.` → `A STICK OF DRY WOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the test, in paraphrase. Moses takes a staff from the leader of each of the twelve tribes and writes each leader's name on his staff. On the staff of the tribe of Levi he writes Aaron's name. He lays all twelve in the Tent of Meeting overnight, and God says the staff of the one He chooses will sprout. In the morning Moses goes in, and Aaron's staff, in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, had "put forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and bore ripe almonds." Three seasons of a tree's year in one night: bud, flower and fruit, all on a dead stick. Moses brings out the staffs, and every leader takes his own back and looks at it. Only one has changed. The Hebrew word for almond is shaked, and the prophet Jeremiah later makes a pun on it: he sees an almond branch, shaked, and God tells him He is shoked, watchful, over His word. So the almond is the wakeful tree. And one more detail: Aaron's staff isn't thrown away. It's put back before the Ark and kept, as a sign for the rebellious, the text says, so that their complaints would end. The argument about who serves is settled not by the loudest voice or the strongest punishment, but by something growing. After a rebellion that started with jealousy, the last word is a living thing that nobody could fake.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for something budding. Settle, and breathe. If there's a window near you, look out of it; if not, look around the room. Find one living thing: a tree, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, even your own hand. Look at it as if it might change overnight. Then turn inward. Is there something in your life that looked dry for a long time and is starting, just barely, to come back? A friendship, a habit, a hope. Just notice it. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Korach. A rebellion that ended with a flowering stick. And this week: forty years in the wilderness, the fringes, and five days with Korach, from a fair-sounding claim to an almond in bloom.
Your line: the staff blossoms. Today, find one sign of something coming back to life, outside or in someone you love, and say so out loud. Day four hundred fifty-five.

original.note: Hebrew: almond, the fruit on Aaron's staff; Jeremiah plays it against shoked, watchful (Jeremiah 1:11–12).
